title: I watched Burning but I realised that my interpretation is completely different from most people's, does someone see it as I do

commenti.body:
I can't understand this one personally.

1. Ben is seen to be grooming a new woman

2. It's implied the items in his apartment belong to a number of women.

3. It's pretty clearly implied that the protagonist believes Ben has kidnapped / possibly killed her or is part of a conspiracy to do so.

4. What would possibly be her motivation for doing this?

The film is littered with little bits of dialogue and clues / small details that do not really lend themselves to your theory.

I like your interpretation a lot! Don’t forget that Jong-su is also writing his novel. He moves into Hae-mi apartment (or was it always his) and we see him typing away. Many scenes filmed are probably from his novel, such as the scene where Ben is grooming a new victim.

3. ok I just didn't get this AT ALL, I think he realised she was a complete liar (her childhood tales being bullshit), saw the watch, and understood that she was living with Ben despite him saying no (the pink watch) -> both of them are liars -> revenge
4. Ben burns greenhouses for fun, she's a similar type of person, but likes to play with people's emotions instead

I don’t really follow this interpretation because it’s not really supported by the text. There is no indication anywhere that Hae-Mi and Ben are accomplices. There is no clear motivation for either her or Ben to trick Jong-Su, and the film never reveals any sort of pay off for this plan. If this is your interpretation, it implies the storytelling in this film is deeply vague and under developed. I don’t believe the film is “tricking” us with a completely different narrative than what’s presented in the text. That to me would be poor filmmaking - relying on gimmicks vs examining thematic questions through compelling characters. 

I do think there is a very interesting exploration of how reliable a narrator Jong-Su is. His character is a very clear commentary on the culture of extreme isolation facing many Korean males, and the ways it influences and twists the way they engage with the world around them. We only know Ben and Has-Mi through Jong-Su’s POV, and so we can reasonably assume his own insecurities and desires could be filtering the subtle nuances of his interactions with them to better serve the story he wants to create in his own mind.

I think the main point of the film is that it doesn't matter. It doesn't matter what exactly happened, that's why it's never fully explained (and why it can't be explained at all).   
  
The mystery serves as a vehicle for the themes - mostly to show the absurd and violent dichotomy between the lower, working class and the higher, wealthy class. The only thing we know is that we see everything unfold from Jong-su's perspective, and even he could be an unreliable narrator (considering he aspires to be a writer of fiction). 

In the end, everything is like the invisible tangerine that Hae-mi eats in the beginning. It's what you believe it to be.

There is no definitive interpretation, which is the point. The protag doesn't have sufficient justification for his belief. It's plausible that she did just disappear due to her debts, but it's also possible Ben murdered her, yet we don't know. Nevertheless, the protagonist is so blinded by obsession and jealously that he accepts the murder narrative with scant evidence because it suits his emotional needs. The film is a commentary on how desire muddies our ability to make objective judgements. It raises core criticisms about justice.

It's fun to argue about what might have happened but it's not worth saying there is a single correct interpretation of the evidence.
ah no obviously theres no right answer, was just curious if someone shared mine

I don’t believe Ben is a killer but I do believe the girl is a liar/“free-spirit”.

1. Ben is a player. 

2. Gets a girl to sleep with him and then saves an item if there’s as a trophy. 

3. The protagonist believes Ben to be a killer but our protagonist seems to be mentally ill. His obsession, overall demeanor, and bizarre behavior in her apartment and stalking both characters. 

4. She’s a girl who likes to act and pretend. Think of the orange scene. If she’s really believes she’s eating and orange then the pantomime action seems more real to others. 

5. I think that the greenhouses are about the women he “burns” through by sleeping with them. Once the fed is done he discards them.

Honestly, I think she just left after our protagonist basically called her a whore. She probably went on another trip. I think Ben is an asshole but that’s it. 

I also don’t think our protagonist kills Ben either. I think it’s in his head and it’s also cut with him sitting at his desk writing. I think that is the end of the story he was writing.

I think you have to question why? What would the motivation be. 

What did Hae-Mi get from tricking Jong-Su. What would Ben gain? Why would they be tricking another girl?

There is nothing in the text to really support what you're suggesting. If anything I think your interpretation would suggest that most of what the film intentionally draws our attention to was in fact not important at all. 

For what it's worth I think there are multiple valid interpretations of the film. The common one is that Ben killed her. I think the reason so many people feel this way this is what Jong-Su literally sees, and I think that's key to understanding the film. The film starts with Hae-Mi performing pantomime. She effectively tells Jong-Su that the trick is to believe the orange is really there. From this point on we're bombarded with conflicting information. Jong-Su lives on the North Korean border and constantly hears propaganda. When he turns his TV on we see Donald Trump. He meets Hae-Mi under strange circumstances and she tells him stories about their childhood we he doesn't remember and struggles to believe. When she goes to Africa, he goes to look after her cat but never sees it. 

Then this strange man enters his life. There is no indication to how he makes his money or why he has such an interest in Hae-Mi. When they go to a gathering together Jong-Su is equally as embarrassed as Ben's friends when Hae-Mi dances but Ben looks enamoured with her. What is it that he sees in her because truthfully, he struggles to see this himself. He doesn't really see her as a person and I don't think he has the self reflection to realise he doesn't have anything going for him himself. In reality they're barely even dating and there is not much to suggest they've interacted beyond the four or five scenes we've seen them together in. In the source text she is a girl on the side if I recall. Yet he is quite possessive and obsessive with her. In their final interaction she tells him and Ben she'd like to disappear before later dancing nude. In their final interaction Jong-Su calls her a 'whore'.

One of the major themes of the film is class. You could probably find hundreds of essays on this but to keep it short, I believe Jong-Su sees Ben as the cause of all of his problems and in his head, he has to reason why Hae-Mi left. He doesn't reflect on why she might have ghosted him. He doesn't reflect on her chaotic and unpredictable lifestyle. He doesn't accept Ben's theories of running away from debt. Like his dad, he doesn't take responsibility for his own situation. So instead he constructs this story and every piece of evidence lines up with it. Or does it?

Take the box of trinkets in Ben's bathroom cabinet where we find Hae-Mi's watch. You think this is evidence that Hae-Mi is in a relationship with Ben whilst others believe this is evidence of further victims. This is where I think the film is at it's best. Because what if this is just a box of trinkets from sexual encounters? How do we know this is even Hae-Mi's? Hae-Mi doesn't wear the watch after returning from Africa. In a previous scene Jong-Su meets up with a colleague of hers wearing the same watch. We're convinced it's Hae-Mi's because Jong-Su is. And then we learn Ben has a cat. Jong-Su suspects this is Hae-Mi's cat and when it responds to it's name being called, this is confirmation that it's Hae-Mi's cat. But we haven't actually met Hae-Mi's cat so how can we be so sure? It didn't previously respond to Jong-Su when he was feeding it so why would it now? From personal experience, cats don't often respond to their name. He maintains this unwavering idea of Hae-Mi in his head which is why he keeps questioning about the well and finally stops after his mother says it was because that fits his narrative. He doesn't challenge much else in the film.

Maybe you're right that Ben really does burn greenhouses for fun. But I think it's pretty clear that when Jong-Su tests this and finds no evidence, he interprets this as a metaphor for killing women. We see him with another seemingly naive woman. We have no context for this, but through Jong-Su's eyes, we assume something more insidious. We receive a mysterious call possibly from Hae-Mi in which a struggle can be heard. The director does something really interesting towards the end of the film and I wonder if you picked up on it. Going back to the whole pantomime thing, Ben tells Jong-Su that he writes therefore is a writer. Towards the end Jong-Su visits Hae-Mi's apartment and gets his laptop out to start writing. The next scene is from Ben's perspective. Every single scene up to this point has been through the eyes of Jong-Su and now we're watching Ben put in his own eye contacts and then applying lipstick to the woman from earlier. So who's perspective are we actually watching here? Ben's or Jong-Su's fictitious imagination? An interesting detail I read a while back is that '화장' is the spelling for both makeup and also cremation. Could be coincidental of course. The final scene starts with Ben's POV also so make of that what you will. 

The film has many themes that I've not even began to touch on and I do believe it's very much up for debate whether Ben had involvement in her disappearance or if Jong-Su even killed Ben. But to me it's pretty obvious that Jong-Su at least believes Ben is involved with her disappearance.
